doc.title: Ran Blake interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, July 16, 2021

title: Naming pieces: 'Memphis' and 'The Short Life of Barbara Monk'
summary: Blake explains how titles come late and the stories behind two recent pieces.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Thank you for that. That makes me feel a little better. Let me talk about song titles for a moment. Do you write pieces with a song title in mind? Or do you name them halfway through or perhaps when they’re done?

Well rarely do I think of it before. I know I’ve written two pieces in the last year that I wish musicians would cover, “Memphis” for Martin Luther King, Jean Plumez, and “The Short Life of Barbara Monk.” With Barbara Monk I remember getting ready to take off at Logan Airport to get to the funeral and I passed out in Boston and I went home thinking of Barbara and her mother Nellie and the whole family and the cousin Jackie Beneaux, and I wrote for his niece [plays piano]. But in “Memphis” I thought particularly maybe shall I call it “Detroit” and my colleague Hankus Netsky, a wonderful recording artist, said this sounds more southern. And then I kept thinking of the assassination in Memphis. And in my various renditions there’s something — we do a melody that I might imagine Al Green doing and then suddenly little things happen like I have a little motif [plays piano] and that comes in very discretely at first and the playing goes on and then it becomes wild as the killer is getting his ammunition all ready with the help of an ally or two, and then, so there are things that are thought through, early pieces like Vanguard are just in space. There’s no real plot. But every time I play it there may be often I play it missing Jeanne because she sang it with me so many times.

Oh that’s very interesting. Some of these thoughts that I have and these questions, I don’t really honestly think they have an answer. Like what does music mean? What can it mean if it’s an abstract art form, especially if there’s no singing? There’s no clear story. So will it affect different people very differently.

I know that I try to have a written program. First it’s sort of a nuisance to people to get them to type it up, and secondly some people arriving at a club just a minute before don’t read the program notes. Once in a while I have the courage to get up and speak or often I have somebody that will represent me. I don’t like to speak much because then I go out of my mood of playing and trying to deal with the audience and when lights go on I get back to the present life. But you’re very, very right, like somebody doing a crash-bang on © Fillius Jazz Archive -9-

Abbey and Max doing — I should mention last names, Roach and Lincoln — doing “Freedom Day.” And somebody just hearing it instrumentally without the words might think it’s, or they may have heard one word, freedom, they may think freedom to get out of school in May. I want summer. I don’t want discipline. So rarely do they get it right. But this might hold the music together for me and other people. I know when my “Blue Potato” came out, my third or fourth record, at the same time Charles Haden’s “Liberation Orchestra” and a lot of it was instrumental. I haven’t heard it for a while. So I think very often it doesn’t convey — when I do “Mendacity” — Max Roach’s piece — and Abbey mentions voting rights they may have just thought — I don’t even know if the people know the background or care and the music meanwhile has to hold up, does it stay together. And there are times I do really, particularly away from the piano, think of the beginning and what I might do as a departure when I go in my world of improvisation, what register of the piano, the role of pedals, and sometimes I follow that and often there’s a different plot, a different character that persuades me to go in a different direction.
